themes.definition: Procedures by which the Commission, prompted by other Member States or on its own view, confirms or overturns national decisions on AI systems, emergency authorisations and notified bodies.
themes.what_is_set_out: Under the Union safeguard procedure, when another Member State objects to a national restriction or the Commission thinks it contrary to EU law, the Commission consults and 'shall decide whether the measure is justified'; if it is, 'all Member States shall ensure that they take appropriate restrictive measures', and if not, the Member State withdraws its measure, while (per the coders' note) a provisional measure is deemed justified if no one objects within three months, or 30 days for banned practices. The same pattern applies to measures against compliant-but-risky systems and to emergency authorisations of unassessed high-risk systems: where the Commission considers an authorisation unjustified, 'it shall be withdrawn' by the national authority. A conformity assessment body may act as a notified body only if neither the Commission nor other Member States object within two weeks (two months without an accreditation certificate), and the Commission may suspend, restrict or withdraw a designation by implementing act if the notifying Member State fails to correct problems. EU043 says all market surveillance authorities 'should follow a Union safeguard procedure with a decision taken by the Commission' on whether a system is a banned practice, so that interpretation is uniform across the Union.
themes.holders: The European Commission (decides); Member States and their market surveillance and notifying authorities (object and act).
themes.binding: Statutory procedures; EU043's 'should follow' is non-binding interpretation. If not met: unjustified national measures or authorisations are withdrawn; designations suspended, restricted or withdrawn.

quotes.quote: the Commission shall decide whether the measure is justified and, where necessary, propose other appropriate measures.
Where the Commission considers the authorisation unjustified, it shall be withdrawn by the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned.
All market surveillance authorities should follow a Union safeguard procedure with a decision taken by the Commission48 determining whether the AI system constitutes a prohibited practice.

The conformity assessment body concerned may perform the activities of a notified body only where no objections are raised by the Commission or the other Member States within two weeks of a notification

themes.theme: Conformity assessment and the bodies that certify tools
themes.definition: The pre-market approval gate for high-risk systems: who assesses conformity, how certificates are issued, refused, renewed, suspended or withdrawn, and how the certifying bodies are themselves designated and controlled.
themes.what_is_set_out: High-risk systems must undergo conformity assessment before being placed on the market or put into service, and EU043 states that 'Providers must ensure their AI systems meet all relevant requirements' first. Where the notified-body route (Annex VII) applies, the body assesses the provider's quality-management system and technical documentation, 'shall refuse to issue' a certificate where the system does not conform (the coders note it may require retraining where training data fall short), and must assess 'any change' that could affect compliance or intended purpose; certificates last at most five years for Annex I systems and four for Annex III systems and are renewed only after reassessment, and a body that finds a system no longer conforms must suspend, withdraw or restrict the certificate unless the provider corrects it in time. The provider 'may choose any of the notified bodies', except, per the coders' note, for systems intended for law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or EU bodies, where the market surveillance authority acts as notified body; the Commission may move Annex III points 2 to 8 to notified-body assessment, which [inference] implies those systems are otherwise assessed by the provider's own internal control. Notifying authorities may notify only bodies that meet Art. 31 and must separate the people who assess a body from those who decide on it; subcontracting needs the provider's agreement, third-country bodies may be authorised under agreements, and when a designation ends certificates can stay valid provisionally (extendable in three-month steps up to 12 months in total). Under the Omnibus the Commission entrusts tests for AI Office-supervised systems to notified bodies acting on its behalf and 'may withdraw the delegation with immediate effect' if they perform inadequately.
themes.holders: Providers; notified bodies; notifying authorities; national competent authorities; the Commission.
themes.binding: Statutory duties and procedures; recitals and EU043 non-binding. If not met: certificate refused, suspended, withdrawn or restricted; designation restricted or withdrawn; delegation withdrawn.
themes.checks: Conformity assessment of the tool. Trigger: before placing on the market or putting into service; on any change that could affect compliance or intended purpose; on renewal (at most every four years for Annex III systems, five for Annex I). Compared against: Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and, for quality management, Art. 17. Metric or threshold: not stated in these passages. Who: the notified body, or the provider under internal control. Result: certificate issued (per the coders' note it must allow 'control of the AI system while in use'), refused with reasons, suspended, withdrawn or restricted; retraining may be required.

quotes.quote: Where the AI system is not in conformity with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, the notified body shall refuse to issue a Union technical documentation assessment certificate
For the purposes of the conformity assessment procedure referred to in Annex VII, the provider may choose any of the notified bodies.
Providers must ensure their AI systems meet all relevant requirements before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

quotes.location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1e); p. 27
quotes.quote: If a notified body to which the Commission has delegated tasks under this paragraph does not perform those tasks adequately, the Commission may withdraw the delegation with immediate effect.

themes.theme: Emergency use of unassessed high-risk systems
themes.definition: Derogations that let a market surveillance authority, or police and civil protection authorities in urgency, put a high-risk system into use before conformity assessment is complete.
themes.what_is_set_out: Any market surveillance authority may authorise specific high-risk systems on its territory 'for exceptional reasons of public security', protection of life and health, the environment or key industrial and infrastructure assets, for a limited period while conformity assessment is carried out. In 'duly justified' urgency, law-enforcement or civil protection authorities may put a system into service without that authorisation, 'provided that such authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay'; if it is then refused, use must stop (the if-not-met field quotes the start of this rule). Other Member States may object within 15 days, after which the Commission 'shall decide whether the authorisation is justified', and an unjustified one is withdrawn. This is a public-sector-specific route around the general rule that high-risk systems should be assessed before use.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities; law-enforcement and civil protection authorities; the Commission.
themes.binding: Statutory powers ('may') with conditions; recital 130 non-binding. If not met: authorisation refused or withdrawn and use stopped.
themes.checks: The derogation postpones the pre-use conformity check. Trigger: exceptional reasons or duly justified urgency. Compared against: the stated grounds and, per the coders' note, a conclusion by the authority whose wording is cut off in the input. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the market surveillance authority; the Commission on objection. Result: limited-period authorisation, or refusal and stop.

quotes.quote: any market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or the putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems within the territory of the Member State concerned, for exceptional reasons of public security

law-enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities may put a specific high-risk AI system into service without the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1, provided that such authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay
the Commission shall decide whether the authorisation is justified. The Commission shall address its decision to the Member State concerned and to the relevant operators.

themes.theme: Setting the standards, codes and benchmarks tools are judged against
themes.definition: Who sets the technical standards, common specifications, codes of practice, testing criteria and benchmarks against which AI systems and models are assessed, and what legal weight these carry.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission 'shall issue, without undue delay, standardisation requests' to European standardisation organisations covering all high-risk requirements; conformity with published harmonised standards creates a presumption of conformity, as does training and testing on data reflecting the setting of use and, under the Omnibus, meeting the Cyber Resilience Act for cybersecurity. Participants in standardisation 'shall seek to' ensure balanced, multi-stakeholder representation, and if standards are not delivered, are late or 'insufficiently address fundamental rights concerns' (coders' note), the Commission may adopt common specifications by implementing act. For general-purpose models and for marking and labelling AI-generated content, codes of practice come first: the AI Office and Board aim to make them cover the obligations, the Commission may approve them with general validity, and if they are inadequate it may adopt common rules; the Omnibus has the Commission assess adequacy 'taking utmost account of the opinion of the Board'. Benchmarks for testing are mostly prospective: the Code of Practice on AI-generated content (EU121) refers to 'methods and benchmarks endorsed by the AI Office', the general-purpose guidelines (EU088) say the AI Office 'will monitor' and if necessary set a common approach for external model evaluators, JRC129100 recommends EU-level 'common criteria for the testing of AI' and impact-assessment indicators tied to internationally recognised principles, and ENISA suggests EU-wide benchmarks for the security evaluation of advanced models. None of the passages states a metric, threshold or test result that a tool must achieve.
themes.holders: The Commission; European standardisation organisations and participants in standardisation; the AI Office and the Board; signatories of codes; for the JRC and ENISA recommendations, not stated (nearest: EU institutions and 'developers of umbrella AI frameworks').
themes.binding: Statutory duties and powers for standardisation requests, common specifications and code approval; harmonised standards are voluntary but give a presumption of conformity; JRC and ENISA items are non-binding recommendations or suggestions ('it may be useful'). If not met: not stated.
themes.checks: Sets what checks compare against rather than running checks. Trigger: n/a. Compared against: harmonised standards, common specifications, codes of practice, endorsed methods and benchmarks (none yet specified in these passages). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the standard-setters named above. Result: presumption of conformity where standards are met.

quotes.quote: the Commission shall issue, without undue delay, standardisation requests covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter
The Commission may adopt, implementing acts establishing common specifications for the requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter
Establish at the EU level common criteria for the testing of AI, following relevant standardisation activities and guidelines.52

it may be useful to establish EU-wide state-of-the-art benchmarks for the security evaluation of advanced AI models, including standardised testing against cyber ranges, exploitability metrics, and simulations of chained attacks

themes.definition: Encouragements and commitments to apply AI Act requirements, ethical principles or management standards voluntarily, beyond what is legally required or before it applies.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers and deployers 'may' draw up codes of conduct, and providers of systems that are not high-risk 'should be encouraged' to apply some or all high-risk requirements voluntarily, with codes based on clear objectives and key performance indicators (coders' note); all providers and, as appropriate, deployers are encouraged to apply further requirements such as ethics guidelines, sustainability and AI literacy, and providers of high-risk systems to start complying during the transition. Recital 27 encourages all stakeholders to take the High-Level Expert Group's ethical principles into account in voluntary best practices and standards. Two EU institutions commit themselves: the Commission says it will 'set a positive example and subject itself to the envisaged rules' before they apply, and the European Court of Auditors says it 'could consider adopting relevant elements of ISO/IEC 42001'. None of these is enforceable.
themes.holders: Providers and deployers and organisations representing them; all stakeholders including industry, academia and civil society; the European Commission; the European Court of Auditors.
themes.binding: Voluntary: 'may', 'encouraged', 'could consider', or institutional self-commitment. If not met: not stated.

quotes.quote: Providers of AI systems that are not high-risk should be encouraged to create codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application of some or all of the mandatory requirements applicable to high-risk AI systems
the Commission itself will already now, set a positive example and subject itself to the envisaged rules.
In addition, we could consider adopting relevant elements of ISO/IEC 42001, the Artificial Intelligence Management System standard (see Annex I).

themes.theme: Human authority to oversee, override or stop a tool
themes.definition: Rules that give named people the power to disregard, override or reverse an AI output, intervene in or stop a system, and that say who those people are and who may modify the system.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act requires high-risk systems to let the people assigned oversight 'decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output', and to intervene or interrupt it through a stop procedure (coders' note), with built-in constraints 'that cannot be overridden by the system itself'; deployers must assign that oversight to people 'who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support'. EU043 adds that overseers 'should also intervene ... or stop the use of the AI system if it does not perform as intended', and in real-world testing 'the predictions, recommendations or decisions of the AI system' must be capable of being 'effectively reversed and disregarded'. The European Parliament's draft framework (EP2024) says 'coordinated containment of AI will be required to ensure it remains under human control', but only 'as a rule' and without saying who exercises it; the EDPS describes, as a possible measure, humans able 'to monitor, modify, or approve decisions in real time', and role-based access control over who may modify a system. ENISA recommends frameworks for AI-enabled security tools that 'prioritise human oversight, auditability, and human-gated triage' and wants solutions that 'keep the human in the middle', yet also observes that human change boards cannot authorise fixes fast enough and that critical service providers 'may be forced to use autonomous patching', a direct tension with human approval. The deployer chooses the overseer; none of the passages says which outputs must be routed to a human.
themes.holders: Natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned (assigned by deployers); providers (design the controls); the human operator; human Change Advisory Boards; national authorities (ENISA frameworks); not stated in EP2024 and the EDPS measures.
themes.binding: Statutory duties for high-risk systems (Arts. 14, 26(2)); recitals, EU043, the EDPS measures and ENISA recommendations are non-binding; EP2024 is a draft internal requirement awaiting approval. If not met: fines via Arts. 16(a) and 99(4) per the coders' notes (outside this cell's passages); otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: Human review of outputs. Trigger: during use, 'in any particular situation'; in testing, throughout. Compared against: whether the system 'does not perform as intended' or risks negative consequences. Metric or threshold: not stated (no accuracy, confidence or error threshold). Who: the natural persons assigned by the deployer. Result: output disregarded, overridden or reversed; use interrupted or stopped. Which cases reach a human: not stated, except ENISA's 'human-gated triage', whose gating rule is not given.

quotes.quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system
Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.
Those persons should also intervene in order to avoid negative consequences or risks, or stop the use of the AI system if it does not perform as intended.

quotes.quote: The “Authority Gap” refers to the inability of human Change Advisory Boards (CABs) to authorise interventions in just the few minutes available to counter autonomous exploits.

themes.theme: No decision on AI output alone; the final decision stays human
themes.definition: Rules and guidance that bar adverse decisions based solely on an AI output, require separate human verification before acting on it, or reserve the final decision to a human.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act's binding rules here are narrow: 'No decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken based solely on the output' of real-time remote biometric identification, the same applies to police use of after-the-event identification, and for biometric identification systems 'no action or decision is taken by the deployer ... unless that identification has been separately verified' (the coders' note on recital 73 calls this two-person verification), an extra check that Union or national law may switch off for law enforcement, migration, border control and asylum where it is considered disproportionate. Recital 61 reserves 'the final decision-making' in courts to a human, and EU043 says that even with authorisation no adverse decision may rest solely on a real-time identification output and that a system which itself 'decides upon the necessity to identify' is prohibited; it also warns, for social scoring, that a human final decision does not make a practice lawful if the AI score 'plays a sufficiently important role in the final decision'. The EDPS tells EU institutions to be 'very attentive to the weight' of system information in the final steps of a decision and to make sure the right to human intervention works, especially for autonomous AI agents. The European Court of Auditors limits AI in recruitment to 'a preliminary assessment' with the final decision 'fully with the selection panels', the Commission states that AI 'must be an instrument of support for staff', and its staff rules forbid directly replicating generative output in public documents, 'notably legally binding ones'.
themes.holders: Deployers and law enforcement authorities (biometric identification); judges; EUIs and controllers; ECA selection panels; Commission staff; not stated in several passages (passive 'It shall be ensured').
themes.binding: Statutory for biometric identification (Arts. 5(3), 14(5), 26(10)); recitals and EU043 non-binding; EDPS orientations non-binding; the ECA and Commission documents are internal commitments or policy ('shall never' for Commission staff). If not met: Art. 99 fines for the statutory rules (subject to national rules for public bodies); otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: Human verification of outputs. Trigger: before any action on a biometric identification; before any decision with adverse legal effect; for ECA recruitment, every AI preliminary assessment. Compared against: not stated (the coders' note on EU043 mentions 'further checks' without a full list). Metric or threshold: 'separately verified'; 'decisive influence' and 'sufficiently important role' are undefined. Who: deployer staff (two persons for biometric identification, per the coders' note); selection panels; Commission staff. Result: action allowed only after verification; the final decision is taken by a human. Which cases reach a human: decisions with adverse legal effect and biometric identifications; otherwise not stated. Confidence scores are not mentioned.

quotes.quote: No decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken based solely on the output of the ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification system.
EUIs must be very attentive to the weight that the information provided by the system has in the final steps of the decision-making procedure
Any such use would be limited to a preliminary assessment, with human review and final decision‑making remaining fully with the selection panels

themes.theme: Operators' duties to suspend, withdraw or not use a tool
themes.definition: Duties on providers, importers, distributors and deployers to stop, suspend, withdraw, disable or not use an AI system when it does not conform, presents a risk or has not been registered.
themes.what_is_set_out: A provider that considers or has reason to consider its high-risk system non-conforming 'shall immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it', and importers and distributors must not place or make it available until it conforms, or must withdraw or recall it once available. A deployer that has reason to think use according to the instructions may present a risk must inform the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority and 'shall suspend the use of that system'. Public authorities and EU bodies face a specific pre-use gate: if a high-risk system they envisage using has not been registered in the EU database, 'they shall not use that system' and must inform the provider or distributor. EU043 adds that providers of general-purpose systems are 'expected to take appropriate measures' when they learn that specific deployers are misusing the system for a banned purpose, which [inference] implies a power to restrict a deployer's use.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk systems; importers; distributors; deployers; public-authority and EU-body deployers (registration gate); providers of general-purpose systems.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall'); EU043 is a non-binding expectation. If not met: fines under Art. 99(4) per the coders' notes (outside this cell's passages).
themes.checks: Trigger: the operator 'considers or has reason to consider' non-conformity or risk; for public deployers, before use. Compared against: the Regulation's requirements; risk within the meaning of Art. 79(1); registration in the EU database. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: the provider, importer, distributor or deployer itself. Result: suspension, withdrawal, disabling, recall or non-use, and notification of the authority. How a deployer comes to 'have reason to consider' a risk is not stated in this cell.

quotes.quote: has not been registered in the EU database referred to in Article 71, they shall not use that system and shall inform the provider or the distributor
they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system
shall immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate
They are also expected to take appropriate measures if they become aware that the system is misused for this specific prohibited purpose by specific deployers, for example, if such misuse is reported

themes.theme: Sandboxes and real-world testing: admission, conditions and stopping
themes.definition: Who decides whether an AI system may be tested in a regulatory sandbox or in real-world conditions, on what conditions, and who can suspend or end the testing.
themes.what_is_set_out: National competent authorities decide on sandbox admission within three months, may extend participation, agree testing terms and safeguards with participants, and 'shall have the power to temporarily or permanently suspend the testing process' where significant risks cannot be mitigated; the Omnibus makes participation depend on 'a specific sandbox plan agreed' with the authorities, and the Commission sets detailed arrangements by implementing act. Personal data collected for other purposes may be reused in a sandbox only for systems 'developed for safeguarding substantial public interest by a public authority or another natural or legal person', that processing must not lead 'to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects', and law enforcement needs a specific legal basis. Testing in real-world conditions outside sandboxes needs the market surveillance authority's approval of the test and its plan, but approval is tacit if the authority does not answer within 30 days (coders' note); tests last at most six months (extendable once), outputs must be capable of being 'effectively reversed and disregarded', subjects give informed consent and may withdraw at any time without justification, and providers must suspend or end testing after a serious incident. Law enforcement may test without consent where seeking it would prevent the test, provided the test has no negative effect on subjects and their data are deleted, and authorities may waive the duration limit and the protection of vulnerable groups. Under the Omnibus, Member States 'that choose to allow' real-world testing of AI in Annex I Section B products must adopt frameworks that include 'a mandatory real-world testing plan' agreed with the authority.
themes.holders: National competent authorities; market surveillance authorities; the Commission; providers and prospective providers; subjects of testing and their representatives; Member States.
themes.binding: Statutory duties, powers and conditions; recitals non-binding. If not met: testing may not proceed; suspension or termination.
themes.checks: Testing in real-world conditions. Trigger: before testing (approval of the plan); on a serious incident; on significant risks identified during development and testing. Compared against: the real-world testing plan and the Art. 60(4) conditions. Metric or threshold: 30 days for tacit approval; six months' duration; no performance or accuracy metric stated. Who: the market surveillance authority or national competent authority; the provider. Result: approval (express or tacit), suspension or termination; outputs must remain reversible.

quotes.quote: the market surveillance authority in the Member State where the testing in real world conditions is to be conducted has approved the testing in real world conditions and the real-world testing plan
National competent authorities shall have the power to temporarily or permanently suspend the testing process, or the participation in the sandbox if no effective mitigation is possible
the predictions, recommendations or decisions of the AI system can be effectively reversed and disregarded.

quotes.quote: include the provision of a mandatory real-world testing plan to be agreed between the provider or prospective provider and the national competent authority or relevant authority

themes.theme: General-purpose AI models: provider status, systemic-risk designation and Commission enforcement
themes.definition: Rules and Commission readings that decide which models count as general-purpose or as carrying systemic risk, when a downstream actor becomes a model provider, which exemptions apply, and the Commission's powers over model providers.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission has exclusive competence to supervise and enforce the general-purpose model rules, entrusted to the AI Office, and may request mitigation measures, 'restrict the making available on the market, withdraw or recall the model', and make providers' commitments binding; it adopts implementing acts on how model evaluations are run, 'including the detailed arrangements for involving independent experts'. A model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities above 10^25 floating-point operations of training compute (extracted as '1025'), providers may argue otherwise and the Commission 'will assess the arguments and decide', and it may designate a model ex officio or on a scientific-panel alert using Annex XIII criteria such as parameters, data, compute, benchmarks and reach; it may also amend the thresholds by delegated act. EU088 sets indicative criteria: a model is general-purpose if trained with more than 10^23 operations and it 'can generate language', its lifecycle starts with the large pre-training run, and a downstream modifier becomes provider of the modified model only if the modification leads to a significant change in the model's generality, capabilities or systemic risk, indicated by using more than a third of the original training compute. Exemptions cover open-source models without systemic risk, models used purely for internal processes (but not processes 'essential for providing a product or service to third parties' or that 'affect the rights of natural persons'), modifications (obligations limited to what changed), and models placed on the market before 2 August 2025, whose providers need not carry out retraining or unlearning where that is not possible for past actions; EU090 sets the scope of the training-data summary and leaves out data used during operation such as retrieval (coders' note). [inference] A public body fine-tuning a commercial model for its own service would usually not become the model's provider on these criteria, though it may be the provider of the resulting system; ENISA adds that 'adequate risk mitigations' for models with advanced cyber capabilities 'need to be identified'.
themes.holders: The European Commission and the AI Office; the scientific panel; independent experts; providers of general-purpose models, upstream and downstream; downstream modifiers and integrators.
themes.binding: Statutory powers and thresholds; EU088 and EU090 are non-binding Commission interpretation, though EU088 says the Commission will base its enforcement on it; ENISA non-binding. If not met: fines for failing to comply with requested measures (Art. 101, per the coders' note); designation brings Art. 55 duties.
themes.checks: Model classification and evaluation. Trigger: when a compute threshold is met, on notification, or on a scientific-panel alert; evaluations as the Commission decides. Compared against: training compute, Annex XIII criteria, benchmarks and evaluations. Metric or threshold: 10^25 operations (systemic-risk presumption); 10^23 operations plus language generation (general-purpose indicator); more than one third of original compute (modifier becomes provider). Who: the Commission and AI Office, independent experts, the scientific panel. Result: designation, acceptance or rejection of a rebuttal, requested measures, restriction, recall. Nothing here concerns checking the outputs of a model once deployed.

an indicative criterion for a model to be considered a general-purpose AI model is that its training compute is greater than 1023 FLOP and it can generate language

the Commission considers a downstream modifier to become the provider of the mo dified general -purpose AI model only if the modification lead s to a significant change in the model’s generality, capabilities, or systemic risk.

themes.theme: Data protection law as a gate on AI: legal basis, purpose, roles and anonymity
themes.definition: Data protection requirements, as read by the EDPS and EDPB, that decide whether and how personal data may be used to develop or deploy AI, who is responsible as controller, and whether a model falls under data protection law at all.
themes.what_is_set_out: For EU institutions, the EDPS says there must be 'a distinct lawful ground for the processing carried out at every stage of the generative AI lifecycle', a valid legal basis before personal data are used for training, a public-task basis 'laid down in EU law', and no reliance on legitimate interest, which 'is not applicable in the context of the Regulation'; the European Parliament's 2020 guidelines likewise require AI systems considered for use to comply with Regulation 2018/1725. Purposes must be set for each lifecycle phase, reuse must pass a compatibility test, institutions must first check whether synthetic or anonymised data would do, should prefer sources other than web scraping, and must stop processing if consent is withdrawn and no other basis exists. Responsibility follows decision power: a controller is whoever determines 'why' and 'how', including an organisation that decides to develop, commission or deploy a generative system, and roles across the supply chain should be assessed before processing, case by case. Whether a trained model is anonymous is for the supervisory authority to decide case by case, against an EDPB standard that the likelihood of extracting personal data, or obtaining it from queries, 'should be insignificant'; if later operation involves no personal data the GDPR does not apply to it, and a controller need not erase every model built on the data unless the model contains them or can be used to infer them. The EDPS also reads fairness as requiring controllers 'to identify, measure and mitigate these biases', without saying how.
themes.holders: EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (EUIs); controllers and processors; supervisory authorities; the EDPB; the EDPS; for EP2020, not stated (nearest: Parliament's administration); EU law (the legislator) for the legal basis.
themes.binding: Restatements of statutory duties under the GDPR and Regulation 2018/1725 ('must', 'obligation'), set in non-binding EDPS orientations and an EDPB opinion; EP2020 is an internal guideline awaiting endorsement. If not met: mostly not stated; supervisory authorities' corrective powers are in the corrective-powers theme (part 1).
themes.checks: Anonymity assessment of models. Trigger: when a model is claimed to be anonymous. Compared against: the likelihood of direct (including probabilistic) extraction of training data and of obtaining personal data through queries. Metric or threshold: 'insignificant' (not quantified). Who: the controller supplies evidence; the supervisory authority decides. Result: the model is inside or outside data protection law. Bias: identify, measure and mitigate, with no metric stated.

quotes.quote: EUIs have an obligation to identify a distinct lawful ground for the processing carried out at every stage of the generative AI lifecycle, during both the development and deployment phase.

quotes.location: p.30, s.5.3 Principle of data minimisation
quotes.quote: EUIs must ensure they have a valid legal basis before using personal data to train AI systems.
the likelihood of obtaining, intentionally or not, such personal data from queries , should be insignificant 37 for any data subject
If the pursuit of the purpose is also possible through an AI model that does not entail processing of personal data, then processing personal data should be considered as not necessary.
